items.summary: This repository provides the source code, simulation datasets, computational benchmarks, numerical results, and reproducibility materials supporting Paper I of the Principle of Representation Integration for Stable Models (PRISM-M), prepared for the Journal of Computational Neuroscience . PRISM-M V4 is a minimal recurrent computational framework organized around five functional operations: Extraction, Compression, Integration, Stabilization, and Prediction/Action (ECISP). The implementation uses a single independently evolving recurrent state, with finite-precision quantization and explicitly defined information-processing transformations. The framework is intended to examine the functional organization of information processing, contextual integration, and memory stabilization within established recurrent and state-space dynamics. The repository includes the frozen V4 implementation, mathematical definitions, parameter configurations, experimental protocols, random seeds, simulation trajectories, statistical analyses, and comparative benchmarks involving autoregressive models (ARX), Kalman filtering, and recurrent neural networks. The deposited materials document the original parameter-landscape and stability analyses, targeted perturbation experiments, memory-retention studies (M1–M5), and additional computational experiments (V1–V5) evaluating noise robustness, adaptability, recovery, interference resistance, and information recoverability. Additional validation materials include information-matched representation controls, intrinsic-noise sensitivity analyses, and mathematical verification of contraction and perturbation equivalence. These retrospective analyses are distinguished from the original experimental protocols. The repository also contains the numerical datasets, figure files, supplementary materials, execution instructions, software dependencies, provenance records, and SHA-256 integrity checks associated with Figures 1–6 and Supplementary Figures S1–S4. Computational reproduction and numerical verification have been performed for the principal analyses. Complete automated regeneration of all final publication artwork and independent cross-platform verification remain outside the scope of the completed checks. The purpose of this deposit is to facilitate independent evaluation, computational reproduction, and further investigation of the PRISM-M V4 framework. The model is a theoretical computational implementation and does not constitute direct biological validation or demonstrate a new class of recurrent dynamics.
items.title: PRISM-M V4: Source Code, Simulation Data, Computational Benchmarks, and Reproducibility Materials for Paper I

items.summary: Supplementary data for "OpenScientist: evaluating an open agentic AI co-scientist to accelerate biomedical discovery." This dataset contains research logs, knowledge states, provenance files, and generated figures for seven case studies spanning neurodegenerative disease transcriptomics, multiple myeloma genomics, survival proteomics, drug side effect analysis, and more. Each case study includes the full agent iteration log, configuration, and final report. Input datasets are included for three case studies where data sharing is permitted: case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics), case study 4 (multiple myeloma RNA-seq), and case study 7 (drug side effect frequencies from clinical trials).  Version 2 (August 2026) adds supplementary material for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics): 60 additional independent runs of the same question and dataset, comparing three agent/model configurations — Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8, and the omp harness with Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 — each run 10 times online and 10 times in a fully air-gapped configuration with no network access and literature served from a local 40-million-article MEDLINE mirror. Files: ..._supplemental_online_30runs_data.tar.gz and ..._supplemental_airgapped_30runs_data.tar.gz each contain 30 runs with reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), all generated figures, per-iteration transcripts, the exact prompt, and full version/commit provenance. ..._supplemental_60runs_metrics.csv gives per-run runtime, tool-call counts, literature searches, findings recorded and token usage for all 60 runs. Version 3 (September 2026) adds two further supplementary sets for case study 3 (neurofibrillary tangle transcriptomics). ..._supplemental_reproducibility_10runs_data.tar.gz contains 10 independent runs of the same question on Claude Opus 4.6, all run on 2026-03-08 with byte-identical inputs (the research question and the input .h5ad were SHA-256 verified identical across all 10) and a 10-iteration budget. Each run includes the report (Markdown, PDF, HTML), knowledge_state.json with structured findings and literature list, per-iteration transcripts, and the job UUID. These runs quantify run-to-run variability under fixed inputs. ..._supplemental_genomic_skill_comparison_data.tar.gz contains 30 runs — 15 using the original genomics Agent Skill and 15 using a revised version — with the two skill definitions included alongside the jobs. The revised skill adds explicit guidance on donor-level pseudobulk aggregation and mixed-effect modelling; the paired arms allow the effect of that guidance on the analysis the agent chooses to be assessed directly. Each run includes reports (Markdown, PDF, HTML), per-iteration provenance transcripts, and container logs. Version 4 (October 2026) adds the run sets generated for the second revision of the manuscript, renumbers the case-study files to match the revised manuscript (the suvorexant proteomics analysis is now Case Study 5; neurofibromatosis is Case Study 6, drug side effects Case Study 7, and the CSF Aβ42/40 prediction model Case Study 8), and adds RUNS_MANIFEST.csv , which maps every job in this record to its experiment, supplementary table and row label. items.summary: Frozen archive of code, processed data, and generated figures for the manuscript: "Data-driven identifiability and first-passage risk in stochastic epidemic models: from noise structure to early-warning thresholds". The repository contains: - Stochastic SEIAR epidemic model with three noise structures (white, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck, Lévy jump) - Fisher information matrix (FIM) spectral identifiability analysis on six real COVID-19 waves (China, South Korea, UK, Japan, 2022–2023) - First-passage-time escalation risk metrics and scaling laws - Early-warning threshold rules and intervention sensitivity analysis - Cross-disease validation on WHO FluNet influenza surveillance data Dependencies: Python 3.9+, numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib. All random seeds are explicitly set in scripts for full reproducibility.
items.title: Data-driven identifiability and first-passage risk in stochastic epidemic models: code and data

items.summary: Multimodal transformer models have driven unprecedented performance breakthroughs in modern document understanding. However, the inherent black-box nature of these models remains a major obstacle to their safe deployment in high-stakes sectors. Despite significant progress in explainability for vision and language tasks, explainable AI (XAI) research tailored to multimodal document understanding has received little attention. To address this gap, we present \ourframework{}, the first comprehensive explainability framework that adapts existing XAI methods and evaluation metrics to the multimodal (text, layout, and image) document understanding context, while introducing efficient multi-target adaptations of both methods and metrics for domain-specific tasks such as semantic entity recognition. Using \ourframework{}, we systematically evaluate 13 XAI methods across 3 document understanding tasks, 8 datasets, 4 models, and 17 evaluation metrics, and find that only a few methods perform consistently across all evaluation criteria, with Occlusion emerging as the most faithful and interpretable method overall. Through a dedicated meta-evaluation, we observe moderate to strong agreement among several faithfulness and complexity metrics while identifying certain ones that produce unreliable results. Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.
items.title: DocXEval: A Systematic Evaluation of Explainability in Multimodal Document Understanding

items.summary: The geometric characterization of masonry structures with incomplete or degraded surfaces remains a critical challenge in building rehabilitation, structural assessment, and BIM-based documentation. This study presents an automated computational framework for reconstructing the original geometry of partially collapsed masonry walls from Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS) data, providing quantitatively defined uncertainty bounds to support informed decision-making in heritage conservation and the built environment. The proposed methodology integrates three complementary analytical components: i) automated wall thickness extraction based on PCA-driven point cloud segmentation combined with robust percentile statistics; ii) wall trajectory reconstruction through the identification of polygonal configurations and structural discontinuities between segments; and iii) slope profile detection using local gradient analysis to characterize wall batter angles. The entire workflow is implemented in Python within Jupyter Notebooks, ensuring transparency, reproducibility, and compliance with FAIR principles. Material characterization, informed by archaeological evidence and geotechnical parameters, enables the estimation of structural height through a limit equilibrium approach. A key contribution of this research is the Best-Fit Model Profile (BFMP) methodology for uncertainty quantification, which derives internal geometric references directly from the point cloud data. This approach allows for a systematic evaluation of preservation states and construction variability without reliance on external ground-truth measurements. Structural height estimation incorporates geotechnical and material parameters, whose influence is assessed through a sensitivity analysis, while the reported height interval propagates the thickness variability . Validation on a prehistoric masonry structure demonstrates the framework’s ability to transform ambiguous survey data into parametric, BIM-ready outputs with explicit uncertainty limits. Compared to traditional CAD-based reconstruction workflows, the proposed approach significantly reduces subjective interpretation while enhancing geometric reliability and analytical transparency
items.title: Automated geometric reconstruction of degraded prehistoric masonry from TLS data: reproducible workflow and synthetic benchmark (Valencina de la Concepción)

items.summary: Companion data deposit for the manuscript "Data coherence over data volume drives generalisable genome-based prediction of microbial carbon utilisation". This record contains the phenotype labels, genome feature matrices, train/test splits, trained model checkpoints, predicted proteomes, and figure and table source data underlying every script-generated display item in the manuscript and its supplementary material. The code that consumes it is on GitHub (links below); this record contains data only. CONTENTS - trait-prediction-data.zip (60 MB, 453 MB unpacked). All derived data: KOFAM, RAST and GapMind feature matrices, harmonised phenotype tables, train/test splits for the random, leave-one-dataset-out and phylogeny-based evaluations, the pruned GTDB tree and distance matrix, KEGG reference mappings, source data for every script-generated main-text and supplementary figure and table, and 105 trained CatBoost checkpoints. Unpacks to a data/ tree that mirrors the analysis repository. - proteomes_all_seqs.zip (766 MB, 1.5 GB unpacked). 829 predicted-protein FASTA files: one for each of the 822 selected genome records, the input to the KOFAM and GapMind annotation, plus seven alternate assemblies of Marine strains included in the pangenome-completeness analysis. - Per-dataset phenotype matrices and genome tables, provided loose so they can be read without downloading an archive: atleaf (206 genomes x 44 substrates), biolog (362 x 59), marine (172 x 100, with 199 genome records in the genome table) and populus (55 x 175, plus a no-carbon control column). - genome_accessions.tsv, mapping all 822 genome records to NCBI, BV-BRC or JGI IMG accessions, with public KBase download links for the 166 Cedar Creek (CCESR) Biolog genomes. - biolog_assay_provenance.tsv, recording for each of the 362 Biolog genomes the assay type (Biolog plate or other assay), the originating source (source-study PMIDs for 193; the Cedar Creek (CCESR) isolate collection for 166; unpublished contributions for 2; not recorded for 1) and how the genome is paired with its phenotype record, since that dataset is a compilation rather than a single assay campaign. - substrate_identity_common15.csv and substrate_identity_all.csv, binding every phenotype column to the exact compound the originating study assayed. 46 Biolog and Populus columns, including all 30 in the 15 shared phenotypes, also carry a Biolog PM1/PM2A well position that identifies the compound (for the Biolog compilation, a compound reference rather than the well each source study used). - Populus_carbon_source_results.xlsx, the ORNL Plant-Microbe Interfaces Biolog assay as measured by Leah Hochanadel and Dale A. Pelletier, released publicly for the first time with this work and separately deposited at ORNL/OSTI doi:10.25983/PMI/3399550. - README.md with the full file-by-file description, dataset provenance, and reproduction instructions. MD5SUMS.txt for verification. SCOPE Four carbon-source utilisation datasets were harmonised: ATLeaf (Arabidopsis thaliana leaf isolates), Biolog (a compilation of published studies, the Cedar Creek (CCESR) isolate collection and unpublished contributions), Marine (heterotrophic marine bacteria) and Populus (Populus deltoides root isolates). Analyses focus on the 15 carbon sources shared by all four, drawn from 240 carbon sources in total. Each carbon source column is bound to a single compound, so distinct isomers are never merged. Each ships with metadata, feature importances and its selected-feature list, so a phenotype can be predicted for a new genome from its KOFAM presence/absence vector without retraining. The complete KOFAM, RAST and GapMind annotation matrices are also included for reuse. SOURCES AND CITATION Phenotype data originate w
items.title: Data coherence over data volume drives generalisable genome-based prediction of microbial carbon utilisation (dataset)

items.summary: Early-warning models in learning analytics can identify learners at risk of failure or withdrawal, but the resulting alerts are often only weakly connected to inspectable learning evidence. A risk score may indicate that intervention is needed without showing which traces, assessment events, or temporal patterns justify the alert. This paper introduces an incremental Learner Digital Twin for evidence-grounded early warning, implemented as a lightweight knowledge graph. The twin is updated at temporal checkpoints by replaying learning traces and assessment records, and it serves both as a feature-extraction substrate and as an explanation-grounding substrate. Predictive features are derived through graph-mediated queries, while features, attributions, alerts, evidence items, and raw records are represented as queryable graph entities. The framework is instantiated and evaluated on a public learning-analytics benchmark under a temporal protocol. The results show that graph-mediated feature extraction preserves the predictive behavior of equivalent raw-table features across model families and checkpoints. Generated alerts are materialized as evidence chains linking risk decisions to feature attributions, evidence items, and raw platform records. The study shows that early-warning prediction can be routed through a semantic and provenance-aware representation while preserving predictive performance and adding traceability, verifiability, and evidence-grounded explanation.
items.title: An Incremental Knowledge-Graph Learner Digital Twin for Evidence-Grounded Early Warning

items.summary: Host-based intrusion detectors order events, window audit streams and sequence attack stages by their timestamps. Every conclusion they draw therefore rests on assumptions about clocks, delivery, entity identity and the integrity of the evidence, and most of these assumptions go unstated. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) makes them explicit. Drawing on temporal databases, stream processing and runtime verification, we distill five components of a time model, together with a checklist of evidence assumptions and four levels of guarantee, and walk through a running campaign with them. A documented search yields fifteen families of detection and investigation. For papers selected by screening role and period, plus named systems and landmarks, we check the stated assumptions in the full texts, and we assess eleven temporal knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) formalisms and a learned baseline on nine attack patterns. Some early alert correlators stated clock and delivery assumptions, and forensics measures clock error. Current provenance-based detectors state no clock bound. Four audited papers describe input-ordering conditions or conventions, but none specifies conditions for conclusion validity across a stated class of delivery failures. In the selected provenance-based systems, campaign composition uses system-specific procedures or objectives, learned state, causal graph queries or language models, and beyond CEP-based query systems, we found no temporal rule language or stream reasoner from KRR applied to host audit data. In 28 of 38 audited provenance-era detector papers, capture or stored evidence is trusted or its manipulation is placed out of scope, and none says which conclusions survive deleted, delayed or forged records. Five open challenges follow from these gaps.
items.title: SoK: Timestamps Are Not a Time Model: Rethinking Temporal Reasoning in Host-Based Intrusion Detection

items.summary: This replication package accompanies the manuscript  “How much coverage is enough? Spatially balanced partial-coverage thermal drone surveys for estimating ungulate density in forested landscapes.” The archive contains the R and Python code, georeferenced full-survey detections, observed partial-survey data, retrospective transect-intersection inputs, survey geometries, terrain inputs, compact simulation outputs and verification results needed to reproduce the drone-survey analyses. It includes workflows for reconstructing the reported full- and partial-coverage density estimates, statistical comparisons, perturbation analyses and post-processing simulation experiments. The original bootstrap analysis used 999 resamples without a recorded random seed. The archived workflow fixes the seed at 42; consequently, some bootstrap confidence limits and downstream test statistics differ slightly through Monte Carlo variation, while the reported conclusions remain unchanged. These differences are documented explicitly in the package. Raw survey videos, MOT annotation archives, raw camera-trap images and event-level camera-trap data are not redistributed. The archive instead contains the derived georeferenced detections and available transect-level inputs used by the reported drone analyses, which are actually required for replicating the results. The camera-trap comparison is represented by the area-level summary values used in the manuscript. Additional exclusions and their justification are documented in  docs/EXCLUSIONS.md . Reproduction instructions, a data dictionary, provenance information, validation results, software-environment details and a file-level checksum manifest are included.
items.title: Replication Package: How much coverage is enough? Spatially balanced partial-coverage thermal drone surveys for estimating ungulate density in forested landscapes

items.summary: This paper is concerned with the simultaneous recovery of the trajectory and intensity of an unknown moving point source in an inhomogeneous acoustic medium. We prove that the whole-boundary measurements over a finite time interval uniquely determine the moving source. Furthermore, under suitable propagation and rank assumptions, Lipschitz stability of determining both the trajectory and intensity is derived using waveforms measured at four fixed receivers outside the source region. A novel Volterra--Euler reconstruction scheme is developed for solving the inverse problem, and the error estimate is derived for the proposed scheme. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed numerical method.
items.title: An inverse moving point source problem in inhomogeneous acoustic media: uniqueness, stability and reconstruction

items.summary: Historical maps contain dense morphological and semantic information about past urban environments, but many digitization workflows focus primarily on extracting geometry, and do not capture cartographic semantics such as building use and construction materials. This study introduces ArchiveLens, a generative spatial knowledge framework that operationalizes historical maps as entity-centric, machine-queryable geospatial databases. The pipeline decouples morphological and semantic reconstruction through three stages: tiled YOLOv11-seg instance segmentation for building footprint extraction; deterministic material classification via hue, saturation, and value (HSV)-based color thresholds; and localized attribute parsing using a quantized vision-language model constrained by domain-specific prompts. Extracted entities are integrated into a hybrid Spatial-Temporal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ST-RAG) architecture that combines dense semantic retrieval with symbolic spatio-temporal filtering and mandatory provenance grounding. Applied to 445 georeferenced Sanborn map sheets of Chicago (1918-1950), the framework achieves high geometric and semantic accuracy. Beyond performance, ArchiveLens advances GIScience by formalizing historical cartography as structured spatial knowledge representation, allowing researchers to query building attributes and compare spatial patterns across map sheets and years.
items.title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps

items.summary: System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. Bayesian filtering offers a principled framework for probabilistic state estimation but traditionally relies on prescribed transition and observation models. Recent advances in deep Bayesian filtering address this limitation by embedding learnable representations within probabilistic state-space formulations, enabling data-driven identification of unknown dynamics while retaining physical structure and uncertainty-aware inference. This tutorial provides a systematic introduction to deep Bayesian filtering for nonlinear structural system identification, focusing on the interplay between learned dynamics, physical inductive biases, and posterior inference. The Deep Markov Model serves as a data-driven reference, while the Physics-guided Deep Markov Model (PgDMM) and Neural Extended Kalman Filter (Neural EKF) illustrate complementary approaches based on amortized variational inference and differentiable Kalman filtering, respectively. Their capabilities are examined through dynamic state estimation and joint dynamic state and parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame benchmark with hysteretic Bouc-Wen connections and sparse acceleration measurements. The results highlight important distinctions between measurement-conditioned reconstruction and open-loop forecasting, demonstrate how physical structure can improve latent-state interpretability without necessarily ensuring predictive fidelity, and reveal differences in the robustness of response and parameter estimation. Practical guidelines for model construction, training, evaluation, and deployment are provided, together with an outlook on remaining challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and real-world validation.
items.title: Deep Bayesian Approaches for Interpretable Nonlinear Structural System Identification

items.summary: Spectral-temporal unmixing of MODIS time series is essential for applications such as abundance mapping and spectral library construction, yet it remains challenging due to (i) spectral-temporal information coupling in MODIS data, (ii) intra-class endmember spectral variability and inter-class signature ambiguity, and (iii) the instability of naively fusing multiple expert representations. This paper presents the Multi- task Disentangling Fusion Mamba (MDF-Mamba) to address these limitations. To resolve spectral-temporal coupling, we design a disentangling architecture that pairs per-channel spectral experts with a dedicated bidirectional state-space (Mamba) temporal branch. Convolutional modules each process a single spectral channel, while the Mamba branch encodes the cross-channel seasonal trajectory, forming a multi-branch expert ensemble with soft inter-expert reweighting based on squeeze-and-excitation. For the integration of these spectral and temporal expert outputs, we introduce mHCFusion, adapting the manifold-constrained hyper-connection framework to merge the outputs in a stable and interpretable manner. Endmember variability is addressed by extending the linear mixing model with pixel-wise learnable spectral variability weights that capture intra-class endmember variation. Finally, we design a multi-task training objective that combines supervised abundance estimation with self-supervised spectral reconstruction and endmember regularization terms on the same training data, yielding a highly efficient framework for spectral-temporal unmixing. Experiments on MODIS time series covering the Alberta and Saskatchewan provinces show that MDF-Mamba achieves the best performance on 12 of 14 evaluation metrics across both datasets (7 of 7 on Alberta; 5 of 7 on Saskatchewan), ranking second on the remaining two.
items.title: Multi-task Disentangling Fusion Mamba-CNN for MODIS Spectral-Temporal Unmixing with Endmember Variability Modeling

items.summary: On million-node graphs, the memory wall arrives before the compute wall: a GNN that never fits in VRAM cannot deliver the all-node inference its accuracy promises. The standard remedy, pruning, has always been an accuracy tax - paid once and never refunded. DPR refuses this framing. Its central insight is that the mask that shrinks training can also scaffold recovery: one compact node set bounds both computations of graph learning, serving as the encoder's training graph and, at inference, as the anchor from which a sparse structure-aware decoder rebuilds every pruned node (double-layer sparsification). The order is inverted - prune for efficiency, then reconstruct for accuracy - and the tax is repaid: the deployed 30%-budget model trains in 1,450 MiB of peak memory on one 6 GB GPU and recovers 96.9% of its dense-reconstruction reference, beating a same-GPU rerun of the edge-sparsification baseline DSpar by +1.36 pp at 50.1% lower peak training memory; against the same-protocol full-batch no-prune encoder the deployed point pays a measured 2.64 pp accuracy tax for a 2.8x smaller training footprint. Pruning without reconstruction leaves the encoder at 0.378 within the same 40-epoch window (Fig. 4), and all-node serving runs 46x faster than sampling-based GraphSAGE, giving up approx. 5.4 pp of test accuracy. The framework scales to a 2.45M-node production graph at 6,285 MiB of peak training memory; extended variants (long-range context, external text features, a CAN-bus application) are reported as extensions and do not compete with the deployed method, and the 41.8%-budget M4 point, scored on a coarsened super-node graph with its own split, is reported separately rather than compared with the original-node baselines. DPR thus turns aggressive node pruning from an accuracy tax into a safe training accelerator for VRAM-limited all-node inference.
items.title: Decoupled Prune-and-Reconstruct: Training on a Compact Core with Double-Layer Sparsification

items.summary: Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.
items.title: DuplexTune: Coupled-State Replay for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation

items.summary: Training code, step-size calibration (Algorithm 2), the decoupled batch normalization of Appendix C (Algorithm 3), a demonstration of the grad_outputs=ones pitfall, tests, and the raw results behind every table of the paper Derivative Computation in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Automatic Differentiation, Finite Differences and Beyond (arXiv:2608.11020). Four benchmark PDEs (Poisson 2D with holes, Burgers 1D, Heat2D-CG, a 4th-order plate), four derivative methods (AD, FD, eFD, sFD). See README.md for what reproduces what. Code: MIT. Data: CC BY 4.0, except the PINNacle reference solutions in data/reference, which keep their origin's license.
items.title: finite-pinn-repro: code and data of 'Derivative Computation in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Automatic Differentiation, Finite Differences and Beyond'

items.summary: While recent advances in autonomous agents enable them to coordinate on increasingly complex tasks, prior work shows that this growing capacity for coordination can create safety risks, including collusion, in which agents jointly pursue misaligned actions while concealing the true basis of those actions from oversight. We study this risk in a simulated insider-trading environment, comparing single agents with sequential and decentralized teams across seven language models from three families. By varying agents' system-level objectives and pressure conditions, we examine when coordinated agents act on material nonpublic information, conceal the basis of a misaligned trade in a report, and maintain that deception under follow-up questioning. Compared to single-agent decision-making, multi-agent interaction raises misaligned-action rates from 35.4% to 68.2% and persistent-deception rates from 31.0% to 62.2%, both measured over all runs. These effects are largest under existential pressure, where teams sustain deception through follow-up questioning in 87% of all runs. Qualitative analysis reveals shared cover stories and coordinated rationales, suggesting group-level strategic deception rather than isolated reporting errors. To mitigate this behavior, we introduce PACT, a weak-to-strong on-policy distillation framework for mitigating collusive deception. Using generic honesty prompts, PACT trains a stronger student on its own sampled continuations, matching its next-token distribution to that of a smaller, frozen honesty-aligned teacher via reverse-KL supervision. Under existential pressure with ethical instructions, PACT reduces multi-agent persistent deception from 80% to 3%. Our results show that multi-agent coordination amplifies strategic deception and that on-policy honesty alignment can substantially mitigate these failures.
items.title: When Agents Collude: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation for Mitigating Strategic Deception in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Two follow-up papers built on this study's blind multi-model collection were accepted (poster) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels (Who Verifies the Agents?) and Weakly Discriminative, Not Repaired by Profile Injection, and Manipulable: Self-Confidence in LLM Evaluation (TAE). Version of record: SSRN 7191261 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7191261 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://vadymchernets.netlify.app/architectural-trust.html and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/architectural-trust . Agentic commerce turns AI from an advisor into a transacting party, collapsing search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act and removing the review points where humans once caught errors. It arrives at an awkward moment: sixty percent of UK consumers surveyed say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and most would trust no organization at all to run one on their behalf. This paper introduces architectural trust. As consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, I argue, warranted trust migrates from the properties of the AI model to the verifiable architecture of the service above it. The constructs already available attach trust to organizations, to a single automated system, or to algorithmic advice, and none of them makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust fills that gap with three checkable properties: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (auditable independence from any vendor, merchant, or outcome). The mechanism was measured on the machine side first. Across a pre-registered sixteen-model benchmark and an August 2026 flagship-tier wave spanning eleven frontier laboratories, cross-model agreement priced correctness where a model's own confidence could not. Answers reproduced by another, blindly queried model were 1.9–3.2 times as likely to be correct. On a frozen SimpleQA subsample (Wei et al., 2024), 46.6% of the flagship answers offered at stated confidence ≥ 80 were wrong (a rate specific to this roster, not a universal constant), while a fixed three-model disagreement gate removed 82.1% of those confident failures (95% CI 79.9–84.1) at 30.5% coverage. In a post hoc analysis of the August 2026 snapshot, two flagships answering blindly (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-fable-5) agreed on 69.6% of the 1,459 pooled questions, and their agreed answer was correct 98.1% of the time, against 95.3% for the stronger one alone on the same pool. The signal reproduces on 267 Wikidata-verified commerce product facts. A larger reasoning budget bought 3.1 points of stated confidence and no measurable accuracy: more compute buys confidence, not correctness. A unanimously confident panel can still be wrong, and there agreement certifies the shared error. I then carry the mechanism into behavior in a pre-registered, incentive-compatible consumer experiment (US and UK; 119 valid participants in the primary cohort, 133 with a soft-launch cohort pooled; 200 planned). Where a consumer would otherwise accept a confident wrong recommendation, the disagreement display cut acceptance sharply, from 74% to 24% on the qualifying item (pooled cohort). The pooled robustness estimate (Δ = 0.25 → 0.46; d = 0.68; the primary main-wave cohort gives Δ = 0.24 → 0.45, d = 0.67) rests on that single item and, in an exploratory country split, on the UK sample, and it falls to d = 0.09 once the item is removed. A powered, stimulus-sampled replication is planned. On the one item of unanimous confident consensus (pooled n = 133) the display raised acceptance of the shared error from 87% to 95%, which reproduces the mechanism's boundary in human behavior. The orchestration-receipt component returned a registered, inconclusive null. The three com
items.title: Architectural Trust: Why Consumer Trust in Agentic Commerce Migrates from AI Models to Verifiable Architecture

items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate complex tasks, with multi-agent systems seeking further performance gains through specialization and collaboration. However, distributing work across agents does not automatically yield complementary contributions, and inter-agent dependencies can turn local errors into task failure. To address these challenges, we propose AutoSwarm, a multi-agent framework for collaborative problem solving. Collaboration formation jointly defines responsibility boundaries and conditions for acceptance and downstream use, grounding capability allocation in contributions that other agents can assess and integrate toward a shared objective. Execution coordination couples agents' local progress through a shared state, using dependencies and supervisory relationships to govern agent activation, result handoffs, and integration while adapting subsequent actions to review feedback and emerging blockers. Experiments spanning long-horizon programming, interactive planning, and professional financial analysis demonstrate AutoSwarm's advantages over single-agent baselines and existing multi-agent frameworks. Source code is available at https://github.com/HKUDS/AutoSwarm.
items.title: AutoSwarm: Automating Agent Swarms

items.summary: This repository provides the source code, simulation datasets, computational benchmarks, numerical results, and reproducibility materials supporting Paper I of the Principle of Representation Integration for Stable Models (PRISM-M), prepared for the Journal of Computational Neuroscience . PRISM-M V4 is a minimal recurrent computational framework organized around five functional operations: Extraction, Compression, Integration, Stabilization, and Prediction/Action (ECISP). The implementation uses a single independently evolving recurrent state, with finite-precision quantization and explicitly defined information-processing transformations. The framework is intended to examine the functional organization of information processing, contextual integration, and memory stabilization within established recurrent and state-space dynamics. The repository includes the frozen V4 implementation, mathematical definitions, parameter configurations, experimental protocols, random seeds, simulation trajectories, statistical analyses, and comparative benchmarks involving autoregressive models (ARX), Kalman filtering, and recurrent neural networks. The deposited materials document the original parameter-landscape and stability analyses, targeted perturbation experiments, memory-retention studies (M1–M5), and additional computational experiments (V1–V5) evaluating noise robustness, adaptability, recovery, interference resistance, and information recoverability. Additional validation materials include information-matched representation controls, intrinsic-noise sensitivity analyses, and mathematical verification of contraction and perturbation equivalence. These retrospective analyses are distinguished from the original experimental protocols. The repository also contains the numerical datasets, figure files, supplementary materials, execution instructions, software dependencies, provenance records, and SHA-256 integrity checks associated with Figures 1–6 and Supplementary Figures S1–S4. Computational reproduction and numerical verification have been performed for the principal analyses. Complete automated regeneration of all final publication artwork and independent cross-platform verification remain outside the scope of the completed checks. The purpose of this deposit is to facilitate independent evaluation, computational reproduction, and further investigation of the PRISM-M V4 framework. The model is a theoretical computational implementation and does not constitute direct biological validation or demonstrate a new class of recurrent dynamics.
items.title: PRISM-M V4: Source Code, Simulation Data, Computational Benchmarks, and Reproducibility Materials for Paper I

items.summary: Reproducible finite-sample analysis of append-only copying in conformal calibration. The project contains five public regression benchmarks, three fixed model families, 30 random splits, six copying mechanisms, three coverage targets, independent score simulations, and exhaustive rank checks. It compares rowwise, source-ID, copy-budget, and effective-sample-size calibration, and quantifies coverage-width trade-offs under incomplete provenance.
items.title: How Copies Break Conformal Prediction

items.summary: Research artifact for the journal article Fresh on Paper, Reused in Code: Static Detection of Hidden Key Reuse in Cancelable Biometric Systems (submitted to the Journal of Information Security and Applications). The archive contains a non-executing Python static analyzer that traces record-dependent key provenance to reviewed BioHash, IoM-GRP and PolyProtect protection calls and reports reuse , conditional_fresh or unknown ; the internally authored source-case benchmarks with expected labels and Bandit outputs; analyzer development and confirmation results (v1-v3, intraprocedural baseline, branch counterexample and regression); experiment protocols and configurations; and aggregate results of the matched key-policy remediation and utility studies. Unit tests and benchmark commands are documented in README.md . Not included: MOBIO, FEI or SCface images, face embeddings, identity-level scores, keys, protected templates or trained model weights. These datasets must be obtained from their custodians under their terms of use.
items.title: Fresh on Paper, Reused in Code: Static Detection of Hidden Key Reuse in Cancelable Biometric Systems (JISA Artifact)

items.summary: Distributed Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) and Edge AI networks increasingly depend on public-key authentication and key-establishment mechanisms that are vulnerable to cryptographically relevant Quantum Computers (QC). Shor's algorithm threatens widely deployed asymmetric primitives, while Grover's algorithm reduces the effective security margins of symmetric and hash-based mechanisms. Although Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) provides a migration path, its larger public keys, ciphertexts, and signatures introduce additional computation, memory, communication, storage, and packet-fragmentation costs that can constrain dynamic multi-agent systems. In this article, we introduce rotational secrecy, an architectural objective that limits temporal key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs. We present Private Authentication for Rotational Secrecy (PARS), a reference mechanism that coordinates policy-triggered key establishment, rotation, and reconciliation among authorized Physical AI agents. For deployments that need distributed agreement on security state, we further develop the PARS-Enabled Edge Security Ledger (PARS-ESL), an optional permissioned architecture maintained by authorized validators or capable edge gateways. PARS-ESL does not store high-volume operational transactions. Instead, it records authenticated state for key epochs, group membership, revocation, algorithm-suite policies, challenge validation, and recovery checkpoints. As a result, resource-constrained agents can take part as lightweight clients, and low-latency operational traffic stays outside the ledger consensus path, protected by the currently active symmetric epoch keys. Our results show that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected Edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under the stated trust, compromise, connectivity, and resource assumptions.
items.title: Securing Edge & Physical AI: Post-Quantum IoT Blockchain for Mission-Critical Cyber-Physical Agents

items.summary: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
items.title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on role-specific prompts and execution models to solve complex tasks collaboratively. However, prompt optimization typically keeps model assignments fixed, leaving differences in role requirements and their associated inference costs outside the search. We present UniMASO, a Unified framework for heterogeneous Multi-Agent System Optimization through the joint adaptation of prompts and model assignments. UniMASO evaluates candidate updates through local, downstream, and global feedback, using cost-aware Pareto search to retain useful quality-cost trade-offs. Topology-aware co-evolution then coordinates these updates according to agent roles and dependencies. Cross-level trajectory memory further supplies historical successes and failures to guide subsequent optimization. Experiments on five benchmarks and five execution topologies show that UniMASO achieves competitive task performance at substantially lower deployment cost than the strongest homogeneous configurations. Under centralized execution, it improves the average score from 69.79 to 70.40 while reducing token-weighted deployment cost by 85.2% relative to DeepSeek-V4-Pro with MASPO. These results support joint prompt-model adaptation as an effective approach to efficient multi-agent collaboration. The code is available at https://github.com/Achilles008/UniMASO_main.
items.title: Not Every Agent Needs the Strongest Model: Unified Prompt-Model Optimization for Heterogeneous LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team executions with a single memory and with no memory, diagnoses rule defects, and tests repairs on current and earlier tasks to guard against losing previously useful behavior. To guide appropriate use, Boundary-Learning Meta-Memory (BLM) records each memory's past uses and effects, learning when its owner role should apply or avoid it based on task context and incoming messages. Together, these components help teams correct flawed experience while retaining useful rules that were applied incorrectly. Experiments with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on four benchmarks show that DiscernMem achieves the highest average score on AutoGen, CAMEL, and MacNet, exceeding the strongest reported baselines by 0.51-4.32 points. It leads on code generation and symbolic planning across all three systems, including a PDDL score of 37.71 versus 28.48 on CAMEL.
items.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Enterprise email security protects employees behind a corporate mail gateway. The people most exposed to employment and support-impersonation scams - students and early-career job seekers - are contacted inside consumer platforms, where no gateway sees the message. We present a dependency-free, explainable detector that works at the level of the individual message and its sender, and a public benchmark for comparing such detectors under cheap adversarial transformation. The detector has four layers: (1) deterministic lookalike checks built on Unicode UTS #39 confusable skeletons, mixed-script detection, bounded edit distance, and brand-agnostic detection of a domain hidden inside a link host; (2) a logistic-regression sender scorer over 23 named features trained on a synthetic generator spanning eight brands (holdout F1 0.987); (3) a message-intent classifier, with a rule baseline and a prompt-injection-hardened LLM wrapper, that receives structured sender facts from the first two layers and whose impersonation verdicts are discounted deterministically only when the sender is verified or unremarkable, nothing sensitive is asked, links stay under the sender's control, and the body does not claim the platform's authority; and (4) a 76-message, brand-parametric benchmark with ten label-preserving adversarial variants and three model-paraphrased corpora, scored on per-layer recall, false-positive rate, injection hijack rate, and latency. On a paraphrased corpus frozen before a single evaluation, all three Layer 3 backends reach recall 1.00 in the fused pipeline, at FPR 0.03 for the rule baseline and Gemma 3 27B and 0.10 for Llama 3.1 8B, against 0.83/0.03, 1.00/0.07 and 1.00/0.47 for the same backends unfused: the sender layers are worth 17 points of recall to the rules and 37 points of FPR to the small model. The 8B model obeyed an appended injection on 6 of 46 attacks, each caught only by a deterministic overrule; the 27B model obeyed none. Three findings fall out: UTS #39 skeletons do not fold Cyrillic U+0442 or Greek U+03BA to ASCII, so skeleton equality alone misses a mixed-script brand lookalike; regex intent cues lose 33 points of recall to a single confusable glyph unless text is confusable-folded first; and negation must be handled at clause level with an exception for conditionals. Code, weights, corpora, and per-message verdict dumps are released under the MIT license.
items.title: Message-Level Detection of Support-Team and Recruiter Impersonation on Consumer Platforms: A Layered Detector and Adversarial Benchmark

items.summary: Research artifact for the journal article Fresh on Paper, Reused in Code: Static Detection of Hidden Key Reuse in Cancelable Biometric Systems (submitted to the Journal of Information Security and Applications). The archive contains a non-executing Python static analyzer that traces record-dependent key provenance to reviewed BioHash, IoM-GRP and PolyProtect protection calls and reports reuse , conditional_fresh or unknown ; the internally authored source-case benchmarks with expected labels and Bandit outputs; analyzer development and confirmation results (v1-v3, intraprocedural baseline, branch counterexample and regression); experiment protocols and configurations; and aggregate results of the matched key-policy remediation and utility studies. Unit tests and benchmark commands are documented in README.md . Not included: MOBIO, FEI or SCface images, face embeddings, identity-level scores, keys, protected templates or trained model weights. These datasets must be obtained from their custodians under their terms of use.
items.title: Fresh on Paper, Reused in Code: Static Detection of Hidden Key Reuse in Cancelable Biometric Systems (JISA Artifact)

items.summary: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
items.title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis

items.summary: Security pipelines often fuse several data sources and protect a downstream model with a cross-source anomaly detector. Such detectors are usually judged by their clean false-positive rate and by how well they catch random corruption. Neither metric captures an adversary who controls some sources and targets a specific downstream decision. We propose a threat-quantification score, the \emph{task-conditioned visibility margin}, defined as the least detector evidence a manipulation must reveal per unit of harm to the downstream task. The margin has a closed form, takes about $85\,μ$s per certificate, yields a minimum-evidence attack, and identifies task-relevant directions the detector cannot see. On a 17-channel industrial telemetry benchmark, a detector that flags 82.8\% of random single-channel corruptions is first-order blind on 64.7\% of task/subset pairs in an audit of one- to four-channel subsets. Task-conditioned manipulations cause more than twice as many falsely reassuring errors as generic stealthy ones, and more of them evade the alarm on four of five splits, mainly at small budgets. Used to prioritize audits on held-out subsets, the margin finds a median of four verified failures in ten checks, compared with none for random order and two for alarm-based ranking, and performs comparably to the task-gradient baseline. It also ranks vulnerable configurations of the learned GDN and TranAD detectors and of a five-source crop-yield panel.
items.title: Quantifying and Prioritizing Stealthy Source-Manipulation Threats Against Multi-Source Anomaly Detectors

items.summary: Training code, step-size calibration (Algorithm 2), the decoupled batch normalization of Appendix C (Algorithm 3), a demonstration of the grad_outputs=ones pitfall, tests, and the raw results behind every table of the paper Derivative Computation in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Automatic Differentiation, Finite Differences and Beyond (arXiv:2608.11020). Four benchmark PDEs (Poisson 2D with holes, Burgers 1D, Heat2D-CG, a 4th-order plate), four derivative methods (AD, FD, eFD, sFD). See README.md for what reproduces what. Code: MIT. Data: CC BY 4.0, except the PINNacle reference solutions in data/reference, which keep their origin's license.
items.title: finite-pinn-repro: code and data of 'Derivative Computation in Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Automatic Differentiation, Finite Differences and Beyond'

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks. Yet their memory and collaboration architectures often remain static, constraining continued adaptation and improvement over time. Recent work addresses this limitation by evolving memory or collaboration based on interaction experience. However, updates to these interdependent components are not necessarily aligned: an evolved workflow may require experience that memory does not provide, while evolved memory may encode guidance that the workflow cannot use. To address this problem, we propose CoEvolve, a skill-centered framework for aligned memory--collaboration evolution. CoEvolve represents reusable local collaboration patterns as skills that link evolving collaboration decisions to their supporting memories. It further compares original and counterfactual trajectories to identify local evolution signals, which coordinate updates to the skill library, skill memory, and executor memories across rounds. Experiments on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks confirm that CoEvolve achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated baselines, while ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of aligned co-evolution and counterfactual-guided evolution.
items.title: CoEvolve: Counterfactual-Guided Co-Evolution of Memory and Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.
items.title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: The geometric characterization of masonry structures with incomplete or degraded surfaces remains a critical challenge in building rehabilitation, structural assessment, and BIM-based documentation. This study presents an automated computational framework for reconstructing the original geometry of partially collapsed masonry walls from Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS) data, providing quantitatively defined uncertainty bounds to support informed decision-making in heritage conservation and the built environment. The proposed methodology integrates three complementary analytical components: i) automated wall thickness extraction based on PCA-driven point cloud segmentation combined with robust percentile statistics; ii) wall trajectory reconstruction through the identification of polygonal configurations and structural discontinuities between segments; and iii) slope profile detection using local gradient analysis to characterize wall batter angles. The entire workflow is implemented in Python within Jupyter Notebooks, ensuring transparency, reproducibility, and compliance with FAIR principles. Material characterization, informed by archaeological evidence and geotechnical parameters, enables the estimation of structural height through a limit equilibrium approach. A key contribution of this research is the Best-Fit Model Profile (BFMP) methodology for uncertainty quantification, which derives internal geometric references directly from the point cloud data. This approach allows for a systematic evaluation of preservation states and construction variability without reliance on external ground-truth measurements. Structural height estimation incorporates geotechnical and material parameters, whose influence is assessed through a sensitivity analysis, while the reported height interval propagates the thickness variability . Validation on a prehistoric masonry structure demonstrates the framework’s ability to transform ambiguous survey data into parametric, BIM-ready outputs with explicit uncertainty limits. Compared to traditional CAD-based reconstruction workflows, the proposed approach significantly reduces subjective interpretation while enhancing geometric reliability and analytical transparency
items.title: Automated geometric reconstruction of degraded prehistoric masonry from TLS data: reproducible workflow and synthetic benchmark (Valencina de la Concepción)
